claims.text: Choice architecture tools can be divided into tools for structuring the choice task and tools for describing choice options.
Designating an option as the default increases the frequency with which it is chosen relative to non-default options.
Four or five non-dominating options provides an initial choice set size that balances preference matching against consumer cognitive burden.
When decision-makers allocate a limited resource across possibilities, they are biased toward allocating evenly across each identified group or category.
The effect of category partitioning on choice is stronger among decision-makers with weaker intrinsic preferences and attenuates among those with stronger preferences.
Informing households about relative energy usage reduced average energy use by 2 percent, but consumption changes diverged based on political affiliation.

evidence.description: The authors organize choice architecture tools into structuring the choice task (what to present) and describing choice options (how to present it).
The authors synthesize evidence showing default options are chosen more often in investment, insurance, organ donation, and marketing contexts.
The authors argue that four or five non-dominating options encourages reasoned consideration of tradeoffs while avoiding choice overload and context-specific preference traps.
Prior studies demonstrated 1/n allocation tendencies across 401(k) investment options, charitable donations, grocery shopping carts, and event probability judgments.
Fox et al. (2005) demonstrated that wine novices diversified based on whether wine was grouped by grape or country, while wine experts were largely unaffected by grouping.
Costa and Kahn (2010) found an average 2% decrease in energy usage following relative usage feedback, where liberal households reduced consumption and Republican households increased consumption.

methodologies.name: Choice Architecture Tool Taxonomy
methodologies.description: A conceptual categorization framework classifying choice architecture interventions into task structuring (alternatives, decision aids, defaults, time, search) and option description (partitioning, attribute design).

limitations.text: The framework does not provide a theoretical account of why the identified tools affect choice.
The paper does not provide a normative analysis of how choice architecture ought to be designed or when to apply specific tools.
Choice architects may suffer from a curse of knowledge, anchoring on their own knowledge and preferences rather than those of the decision makers.

future_work.text: Investigate the behavioral effects of full open disclosure of choice architecture and potential influences to decision makers.
Create and use individual-level data to calibrate behavioral economic models of choice architecture for policy purposes.
